stem: Which statement best explains how the Bessemer process and the railroads fed each other's growth?

stimulus.source_note: Nineteenth-century engraving of a Bessemer converter in operation, Wikimedia Commons. Public domain. https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Bessemer_process.jpg
stimulus.text: The image shows a Bessemer converter at work inside a steel mill. A large pear-shaped vessel throws off a shower of white-hot sparks as air blasts through molten iron. A ladle and tools lie in the foreground. The converter is the tall upright vessel in the center.

options.text: Railroads stopped buying steel once the first transcontinental line was finished
options.misconception: Background: railroads kept buying steel for decades after 1869; by 1882 most American steel went into rails.

options.text: The Bessemer process made steel so cheap that railroads no longer needed iron ore or coal
options.misconception: Background: making steel still needed iron ore and coal; the process only made turning iron into steel cheaper.

options.text: Steel mills moved west to build rails, so eastern factories closed down
options.misconception: Background: the great steel mills stayed in the East, around Pittsburgh; they shipped rails west, they did not move west.

options.text: Cheap steel let railroads lay more track, and more track meant more orders for steel mills

rationales.A: Background: the railroads kept laying track long after 1869, and steel rails were their biggest purchase. The first transcontinental line was a beginning, not an end.
rationales.B: Background: the Bessemer process changed how iron became steel; it did not remove iron ore and coal from the recipe. Mills still needed both in huge amounts.
rationales.C: Background: the big steel mills stayed in the East, near coal and iron ore, and shipped rails west by train. Eastern factories did not close down.
rationales.D: Background from the books: cheap steel made long rail lines affordable, and every new mile of track ordered more steel. The mills and the railroads grew by feeding each other.
rationales.general:
Picture a loop, not a line.
1. Background: cheap steel cut the price of rails, so railroads could afford to lay far more track.
2. Background: every new mile of track was a new order for the steel mills, and by 1882 most American steel went into rails.
3. Background: more orders meant bigger mills and cheaper steel, and the loop ran again.
Remember: when two industries buy from each other, each one's growth feeds the other's.
